# Lessons for Future Reference

## About the domain (steel-scheduling AI literature)
- The field currently treats energy efficiency, robustness, and explainability as **separate**
  research tracks (17 / 4 / 3 papers respectively) — almost no work integrates all three, even
  though the field's own perspective/review papers say that's what practitioners need.
- "Real industrial validation" (a named plant co-author or real production data) is rare (5 of
  31 papers) but is what most raises a paper's credibility in this field — worth prioritizing in
  any future search or pilot design.
- Recency matters here: the DRL and Digital Twin clusters skew heavily toward 2024–2026,
  meaning the "state of the art" in this domain is still actively shifting — a search done even
  a year from now will likely change the picture.

## About doing this kind of analysis
- **Always verify what a document set actually is before analyzing it as something else.**
  This corpus was initially framed as "incomplete blueprints" — it was actually 31 finished,
  published papers. Acting on the wrong framing would have produced a "progress tracker" for
  documents that had no progress state at all.
- **PDF metadata cannot be trusted at face value.** 9 of 31 files here had blank Title/Author
  fields; anything that consumes metadata downstream (a citation manager, a search index) needs
  a manual cross-check step, not a straight extraction.
- **A curated document set is not the same as a complete literature base.** The "gap" found here
  (no DRL+DT+XAI paper) is a real structural finding *within this set* — but this set looks
  hand-assembled, not exhaustive, so the gap should be verified against a systematic database
  search (Scopus/Web of Science) before it's treated as a confirmed white space in the field.
- **Mapping overlaps (a network view) surfaces gaps faster than reading papers linearly** —
  the empty three-way intersection in Task 2 was the single most useful finding in this whole
  exercise, and it only became visible once the corpus was mapped as a graph rather than a list.

# Task 1 — Inventory & Initial Scan

## Automated metadata extraction
Ran `pdfinfo` + `pdftotext` (page 1) across all 31 PDFs to pull Title, Author, Journal/Venue,
Date, Pages, and an opening snippet. **9 of 31 files had blank Title/Author in their embedded
PDF metadata** (mostly LaTeX-built files where `hyperref` never set `\pdftitle`) — these were
recovered manually from each paper's own citation header on page 1. Full structured output:
see `steel_scheduling_literature_catalog.xlsx` (Catalog tab = all 31 rows; Category Summary tab
= counts per cluster).

## Boundaries of the knowledge domain
All 31 documents are published academic papers (journal articles + conference papers,
2016–2026). They sit inside one bounded domain:
**AI- and optimization-driven production scheduling in the steel/metals industry**, organized
around three recurring sub-goals: energy efficiency, robustness to uncertainty, and
explainability of the scheduling AI's decisions.

## Tools brought to the problem
- `pdfinfo` / `pdftotext` — structural metadata + text extraction
- Manual cross-check against each paper's citation header — metadata gap recovery
- `openpyxl` — structured catalog with category + maturity tagging
- Close reading of abstracts/introductions — category and maturity classification (see Task 2–4)

*(Kept intentionally brief per your instruction to prioritize tokens on Tasks 2–5.)*

# Task 2 — Topographical Mapping

## Hierarchical topic tree

```
Steel/Metals Production Scheduling (AI & Optimization) — 31 docs
├── Classical / Metaheuristic Scheduling — 17 docs (55%)
│   ├── Energy-focused: idle-energy minimization, ladle dispatching, hybrid flow shop,
│   │                    batch heat-treatment, reheat-furnace scheduling
│   ├── Robustness-focused: stochastic machine breakdown, release-time forecasting,
│   │                        robust hot-strip-mill optimization
│   └── Theoretical/algorithmic: polynomial-time algorithms, online algorithms,
│                                  general (non-steel) green scheduling theory
├── Digital Twin / IoT — 4 docs (13%)
│   ├── Furnace-focused: parallel walking-beam reheating, hot-rolling digital-twin agent
│   └── Integrated planning: IoT + key-parameter prediction (CSR case study),
│                              DT + Deep-Q live decision-making
├── Deep Reinforcement Learning — 4 docs (13%)
│   ├── Single-agent: two-stage energy optimization, electricity-spot-market scheduling
│   ├── Multi-agent: demand response / energy management
│   └── LLM-assisted: RLHF for job-shop scheduling
├── Explainable AI (XAI) for Scheduling — 3 docs (10%)
│   ├── Counterfactual explanations for process-prediction-driven scheduling
│   ├── Adapted XAI techniques for explaining a genetic algorithm
│   └── Explainable DRL for production control  ← bridges DRL
└── Review / Conceptual — 3 docs (10%)
    ├── XAI transparency & explainability review (literature review)
    ├── Human-centric Job-Shop I5.0 framework (conceptual, not a model)
    └── Process safety 4.0 (AI perspective piece — adjacent, off-core)
```

## Cross-reference network — where knowledge is concentrated vs. isolated

**Concentrated:** the Classical/Metaheuristic cluster (17/31 papers) — mature, well-trodden,
mostly energy- or robustness-driven optimization models, several validated against real plant
data (ArcelorMittal Tubarão, Shougang Jingtang Iron & Steel).

**Bridge nodes** (papers connecting two clusters):
- *Explainable Deep RL for Production Control* → DRL ↔ XAI
- *Towards live decision-making... Digital Twins and Deep-Q-Learning* → Digital Twin ↔ DRL
- *Research on modelling and optimization of hot rolling scheduling* (digital-twin agent) →
  Digital Twin ↔ Classical

**Isolated node:** *Process safety 4.0* — no citation or thematic link back into the scheduling
core; it's a general AI-in-process-safety perspective piece that happens to share the word "AI."

**The structural finding:** no single paper occupies the intersection of all three of
DRL + Digital Twin + XAI simultaneously. The closest any paper gets is a two-way bridge. That
triple intersection is empty — a real structural gap, not just a reading impression (see Task 3
and Task 4).

# Task 3 — Synthesis Divergence

Drilling into the three sub-topics from Task 2's tree and deliberately contrasting the
approaches within each — the tension between them is what an organization actually has to
choose between, not just read about.

## Tension 1 — How to pursue energy efficiency
| | Classical / Metaheuristic optimization | Deep Reinforcement Learning |
|---|---|---|
| Strength | Mathematical guarantees, interpretable rules, well-validated on real plants (e.g. ArcelorMittal by-product-gas paper) | Adapts in real time to conditions no fixed model anticipated (breakdowns, price spikes) |
| Weakness | Struggles to scale/re-solve fast enough for live, high-dimensional plant states | Black-box: no guarantee, and no built-in explanation of *why* a schedule was chosen |
| **Trade-off** | **Performance guarantees vs. real-time adaptability** — you largely cannot have both from a single paper in this corpus today |

## Tension 2 — How to handle uncertainty
| | Robust optimization | Stochastic / learning-based approaches |
|---|---|---|
| Strength | Worst-case guarantee — schedule holds even under bad-case breakdowns/prices | Better *average-case* performance; doesn't over-plan for rare worst cases |
| Weakness | Often conservative — leaves efficiency on the table in the common case | No guaranteed floor — a rare bad scenario can be handled poorly |
| **Trade-off** | **Guaranteed safety margin vs. average efficiency** |

## Tension 3 — How to pursue explainability
| | Post-hoc XAI (counterfactuals) | Explaining the algorithm's own logic (adapted-GA XAI) |
|---|---|---|
| Strength | Can be bolted onto an existing black-box model without retraining it | Explanation is more faithful — it reflects what the algorithm is actually doing internally |
| Weakness | Explanation approximates the model; may not always reflect its *true* internal reasoning | Only works for algorithms whose internal logic is legible in the first place (harder for DRL) |
| **Trade-off** | **Ease of retrofitting vs. fidelity of the explanation** |

## A fourth, organizational tension worth naming
Papers with a named industry co-author (ArcelorMittal, Shougang Jingtang) or real production
data are the most credible evidence of "this actually works" — but they're also the most tied
to one specific plant's configuration, and least generalizable. The generalizable, theoretical
papers (e.g. the parallel-machine green-scheduling paper) prove less about any one real plant.
**An organization has to decide whether it wants proof that transfers, or proof that's
site-specific and trustworthy for its own line.**

# Task 4 — Integrative Synthesis: A Unified Blueprint

Re-converging Task 3's tensions into one architecture. The empty intersection identified in
Task 2 (no paper combines DRL + Digital Twin + XAI) is exactly where this blueprint sits — it
borrows a validated piece from each cluster rather than inventing from scratch.

## Proposed architecture

```
 [Plant sensors / IoT layer]
          │
          ▼
 [Digital Twin] ── virtual plant model, real-time state
          │           (borrows: DT architecture from the IoT/CSR
          │            and parallel-walking-beam-furnace papers)
          ▼
 [Metallurgical Constraint Layer] ── deterioration effects, reheat
          │                          windows, ladle logistics, no-idle
          │                          constraints (borrows: constraint
          │                          formulations from the Classical
          │                          cluster's 17 papers)
          ▼
 [DRL Scheduling Agent] ── proposes the schedule, optimizing energy +
          │                tardiness + robustness jointly
          │                (borrows: state/action/reward design from
          │                the DRL cluster's 4 papers)
          ▼
 [XAI Explanation Layer] ── translates the DRL agent's choice into a
          │                 human-readable justification, e.g.
          │                 counterfactual ("would have picked X if Y")
          │                 (borrows: counterfactual-explanation method
          │                 from the XAI cluster's 3 papers)
          ▼
 [Human Operator] ── reviews, approves, or overrides
          │
          ▼
 [Actuation] ── schedule executes on the plant
          │
          └────────────► feeds back into sensors/IoT layer (closed loop)
```

## Why this is the *logical* convergence, not just a mashup
- The **metallurgical constraint layer sits between the Digital Twin and the DRL agent** on
  purpose: none of the 4 DRL papers in this corpus encode metallurgical constraints as directly
  as the Classical cluster does — that's the weakest link if skipped, and the Task 3 "guarantee
  vs. adaptability" tension is exactly why it can't be left to the DRL agent alone.
- The **XAI layer sits after the DRL agent, not baked into it** — consistent with Task 3's
  finding that post-hoc XAI is easier to retrofit onto an existing black-box, at some cost to
  explanation fidelity. That's a deliberate trade-off, not an oversight — flag it as a known
  limitation in the Task 5 briefing.
- The **human-in-the-loop review step** exists because none of the 31 papers demonstrate a
  fully autonomous, unreviewed deployment — every real-plant validation in this corpus keeps a
  human decision point.

## Honest caveat
This blueprint is a **synthesis of what the literature validates separately**, not something
any single paper here has tested end-to-end. That should be stated plainly in the executive
report (Task 5) — it's a proposed pilot direction, not a proven system.

# Task 5 — Executive Briefing: Toward Explainable, Energy-Efficient Steel Scheduling

## Attention — the cost problem is not going away
Steel production is one of the most energy-intensive industrial sectors, and every energy-focused
paper in this review (17 of 31 documents) is a response to the same pressure: rising energy
costs and decarbonization mandates. This is not a niche concern — it is the majority topic of
the literature reviewed.

## Interest — recent AI methods promise real, adaptive gains
The most recent work in this review (2025–2026) shows Deep Reinforcement Learning, paired with
Digital Twins, achieving something classical optimization structurally cannot: adapting a
schedule in real time to live conditions — machine breakdowns, electricity spot-market prices,
demand shifts — rather than re-solving a fixed model from scratch. This is a genuine advance
over the (still valuable, still more mature) classical optimization cluster.

## Desire — but trust is the missing piece, and it's fixable
Here is the finding that should shape the roadmap: **not one paper in this 31-document corpus
combines DRL, Digital Twins, and Explainable AI together.** The capability exists in pieces —
DRL scheduling exists, Digital Twin scheduling exists, XAI-for-scheduling exists — but no one
has connected all three. That gap is precisely the adoption blocker three papers in this
corpus name directly: operators do not trust, and organizations cannot safely audit, a
black-box scheduling decision. Closing that gap is not speculative invention — it's assembling
validated pieces (Task 4's blueprint) that already work individually.

## Action — a scoped, four-step path
1. **Narrow to one sub-process first** (e.g. reheat-furnace scheduling) rather than the whole
   plant — every validated paper in this corpus started narrow.
2. **Build the pilot on the Task 4 architecture**, reusing existing validated components
   (DT design, constraint formulation, DRL reward design, counterfactual-XAI method) instead of
   building any of the four layers from scratch.
3. **Validate against a real or realistic benchmark** — the credibility bar in this field is set
   by papers with an industry co-author or real production data (ArcelorMittal, Shougang
   Jingtang); a synthetic-only benchmark will read as less credible to this field's reviewers.
4. **Target venues consistent with this literature** — Computers & Industrial Engineering,
   Applied Energy, Expert Systems With Applications, IEEE Trans. Industrial
   Informatics/Electronics — since that is where this corpus's own quality bar was set.

*Caveat carried forward from Task 4: this is a proposed direction synthesized from what the
literature validates separately, not a system that has been tested end-to-end anywhere in this
corpus.*
